tip: Écrire (to write) is irregular: j'écris, tu écris, il écrit, nous écrivons, vous écrivez, ils écrivent. Note the 'v' in plural.
Use 'être' for professions. In French, no article before the profession: Elle est médecin (not 'elle est une médecin').
'Avoir honte de' = to be ashamed of. Yet another 'avoir' expression where English uses 'to be'.
'Faire' = to do/make. Irregular: je fais, il fait, nous faisons, ils font. Used in many fixed expressions.
Faire (to do/make) is irregular: je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font. Used in many expressions.
'Venir de + infinitive' means 'to have just done something': je viens de manger = I just ate.
Croire (to believe/think) is irregular: je crois, tu crois, il croit, nous croyons, vous croyez, ils croient.
'Aller chercher' = to go get/fetch. A common compound with aller + infinitive.
'Avoir soif' = to be thirsty. French uses 'to have thirst', not 'to be thirsty'.
'Être en retard' vs 'être en avance' (early). Both use 'en' before the noun.
'Aller' is used for health: 'Tu vas bien ?' = Are you doing well? Literally 'You go well?'
Dire (to say/tell) is irregular: je dis, tu dis, il dit, nous disons, vous dites, ils disent. Note the irregular 'vous dites'.
Voir (to see) is irregular: je vois, tu vois, il voit, nous voyons, vous voyez, ils voient. Note the 'oy' in plural forms.
Venir (to come) is irregular: je viens, tu viens, il vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils viennent. 'Venir de' = to come from.
'Mettre' = to put/set. Irregular: je mets, tu mets, il met. 'Mettre la table' = to set the table.
Sortir (to go out) is irregular like partir: je sors, tu sors, il sort, nous sortons. Don't confuse with 'quitter' (to leave a place).
'Conduire' = to drive. Irregular: je conduis, tu conduis, il conduit. 'Trop vite' = too fast.
Recevoir (to receive) is irregular: je reçois, tu reçois, il reçoit, nous recevons, vous recevez, ils reçoivent. Note the cedilla.
'Être en train de' + infinitive = to be in the process of doing something. Emphasizes the ongoing nature.
Use 'avoir' for physical features: avoir les cheveux bruns (to have brown hair), avoir les yeux verts (to have green eyes).
'Où se trouve...?' = Where is...located? More formal than 'Où est...?' Both are correct.
'Que' becomes 'qu'' before a vowel: 'Qu'est-ce que...', 'Qu'avez-vous...'

target: Est-ce que le magasin est ouvert ?
tip: 'Ouvert' is the past participle of 'ouvrir'. Used as an adjective: le magasin est ouvert.

target: Est-ce que vous avez une chambre ?
tip: 'Est-ce que' is the easiest way to form questions – just add it before a statement. No word order change needed.
je → j' before a vowel or silent h: j'aime (I love), j'habite (I live). Elision is mandatory – je aime is wrong.
Aller (to go) is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il/elle va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont. 'Au' = à + le (contraction).
Mettre (to put/put on) is irregular: je mets, tu mets, il met, nous mettons, vous mettez, ils mettent. Double 't' in plural.
'À l'aéroport' uses the contracted 'à l'' before vowels. Full form would be 'à le', but that doesn't exist.
'Beau/belle' is one of the BANGS adjectives that go before the noun: 'une belle maison', not *'une maison belle'.
Courir (to run) is irregular: je cours, tu cours, il court, nous courons, vous courez, ils courent. Only one 'r' in present.
Suivre (to follow) is irregular: je suis, tu suis, il suit, nous suivons, vous suivez, ils suivent. Same 'je suis' as être – context decides.
'Chez' means 'to/at the place of'. Use with people: chez le médecin, chez moi (at my place), chez Paul.
'Avoir l'habitude de' = to be used to. French 'has the habit of' doing something.

english: An hour is enough for me.
tip: 'Il me suffit de' = it suffices for me / is enough for me. Same reverse pattern: il te suffit de, il lui suffit de.

english: They have a lot of patience.
tip: 'Beaucoup de' (much/many) is always followed by 'de', never 'des': beaucoup de patience, beaucoup d'amis.

target: Ils ont soif après le match.
english: They are thirsty after the game.
tip: French says 'I have hunger' (`j'ai faim`), not 'I am hungry'. Same with `j'ai soif`, `j'ai froid`, `j'ai peur`, `j'ai 30 ans`. Sensations and age use `avoir`, not `être`.

english: What do you want to drink?
tip: 'Boire' is highly irregular: je bois, tu bois, il boit, nous buvons. Past participle: bu.

target: Nous avons faim après la randonnée.
english: We are hungry after the hike.
tip: Watch these: faim, soif, chaud, froid, sommeil, peur, raison, tort, honte, de la chance. All take `avoir`. Saying `je suis faim` would mean you are hunger.

english: Do you have a menu in English?
tip: 'Avoir' in inversion: 'avez-vous des enfants?' Formal question form. 'Des' = some (partitive).

target: Elle sort du bureau à cinq heures.
english: She leaves the office at five.
tip: 'Sortir' = to go out/leave. Irregular -ir: je sors, il sort. 'Du' = de+le: 'sort du bureau' = leaves the office.

target: À quelle heure ferme le musée ?
english: What time does the museum close?
tip: 'À quelle heure...?' = At what time...? Use to ask about schedules: À quelle heure part le train ?
'Avoir tort' = to be wrong, 'avoir raison' = to be right. French 'has wrong/reason'.
Use 'être' for marital status: je suis marié(e), je suis célibataire, je suis divorcé(e).
'Être en forme' = to be in shape/fit. A useful everyday expression.
'Être fier de' = to be proud of. The adjective agrees: fier/fière.
Use 'être' for nationality: je suis français(e), tu es anglais(e). The adjective agrees with the subject's gender.
'Être d'accord' = to agree. Literally 'to be of agreement'. Very common expression.
'Être en colère' = to be angry. Use 'être' for emotional states: être triste, être content, être en colère.
'Avoir confiance en' = to trust / to have confidence in. Another avoir expression for a feeling.
'Gentil' adds an extra -le in feminine: gentil/gentille. The pronunciation changes significantly.
'Être en vacances' = to be on vacation. Note the plural 'vacances' – always plural in French.
'Avoir mal à' + body part = to hurt: 'j'ai mal au ventre'. The article contracts: à + le = au.
'Quelle heure est-il ?' is the standard way to ask the time. 'Heure' is feminine, so use 'quelle'.
'De l'' is the partitive before vowels: de l'eau, de l'huile, de l'argent. Same meaning as du/de la: 'some'.
Age uses `avoir`: `j'ai 25 ans` = literally 'I have 25 years'. Direct translation from English would be wrong.
'C'est loin' uses 'c'est' (it is) for describing distance. Very common in everyday French.
Use 'être' for location: je suis à Paris, il est au bureau, nous sommes ici.
'Qu'est-ce que' = what (as object). Literally 'What is it that'. Used for asking about things/actions.
`on` is the all-purpose informal 'we' in spoken French: `on va au cinéma` = 'we're going to the movies' (not `nous`). Verbs conjugate as 3rd singular even though it means 'we'.
'Quel/quelle' = Which/What. Agrees with the noun: quel (masc.), quelle (fem.), quels (masc. pl.), quelles (fem. pl.).
